topic: Linear Algebra: The Soul of Matrices (Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues, and Eigenbasis)
target_audience: University STEM students or advanced high school students with a basic understanding of matrices.

sections.title: Introduction: The 'Stretchy Cat' Hook
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a linear transformation using a visual metaphor. Most vectors change direction when a matrix is applied, but a special few do not. This sets the stage for defining 'Eigen' (meaning 'own' or 'characteristic').
sections.example: Imagine a 2D picture of a cat on a coordinate plane. If we apply a 'shear' transformation (tilting the cat), most points move to new lines. However, the cat's whiskers along the horizontal axis might stretch but stay on the exact same horizontal line. These whiskers are like eigenvectors.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: Matrices as Functions
sections.content: Briefly review matrix-vector multiplication (Av = w) as a geometric transformation. Visualize a grid being warped: squares turning into parallelograms. Define 'Linear Transformation' visually.
sections.example: An animation showing a standard grid (i, j) transforming into a skewed grid. A vector (1, 1) is shown moving to a new position (3, 2) after being multiplied by a matrix A.

sections.title: Core Definitions: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
sections.content: Formally introduce Av = λv. Explain that an eigenvector (v) is a non-zero vector whose direction remains unchanged by the transformation. The eigenvalue (λ) is the 'scale factor' by which it is stretched, squeezed, or flipped.
sections.example: Graphical representation: A vector 'v' pointing at (1,1). After matrix multiplication, it lands at (2,2). Here, v is the eigenvector and λ = 2 because it simply doubled in length without changing its span.

sections.title: The Math Behind the Magic: Characteristic Equation
sections.content: Explain how to find these values using det(A - λI) = 0. Show that solving for λ gives the 'characteristic' scale factors of the matrix. This connects the geometric intuition to algebraic calculation.
sections.example: Using a simple 2x2 matrix A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. Step through the subtraction of λ from the diagonal and finding the determinant to solve the quadratic equation (λ-3)(λ-1)=0.

sections.title: The Power of Eigenbasis
sections.content: Introduce the Eigenbasis: a coordinate system made entirely of eigenvectors. Explain that in this 'custom' coordinate system, the matrix transformation becomes a simple diagonal matrix, making complex operations (like matrix powers) incredibly easy.
sections.example: A 'Change of Perspective' animation. Instead of using the standard X and Y axes, we rotate our view so the axes align with the eigenvectors. In this new view, the transformation looks like a simple independent stretch in two directions.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Bridge Resonance
sections.content: Conclude by showing why this matters. Mention how eigenvalues represent the 'natural frequencies' of a system, such as a bridge or a building.
sections.example: An animation of a bridge. The eigenvectors represent the shape of the bridge's vibration modes, and the eigenvalues represent the frequencies. If wind hits the bridge at an eigenvalue frequency, resonance occurs (like the Tacoma Narrows Bridge).
